details:
**Aconcagua**
The highest peak in the Andes and in the Americas, at about 22,840 feet, in Argentina's Mendoza Province. It is the second-highest of the Seven Summits, and its name may come from Mapudungun, the language of the Mapuche. Matthias Zurbriggen made the first ascent in 1897 by way of the Valle de las Vacas ("Valley of the Cows"), and the peak's Polish Glacier is a well-known climbing route.

**Chimborazo**
An inactive volcano in Ecuador. Because Earth bulges at the equator, its summit is the farthest point on Earth's surface from the planet's center, though it is far from the highest peak above sea level.

**Salar de Uyuni**
The world's largest salt flat, on the Bolivian Altiplano near the town of Uyuni. It holds a large share of the world's lithium reserves, and flamingos breed in the area.

**Lake Titicaca**
A large lake on the Altiplano on the border of Peru and Bolivia, often called the highest navigable lake in the world. The ancient city of Tiwanaku developed near its southern shore.

**Subduction of the Nazca Plate**
The Andes formed, and are still rising, as the oceanic Nazca Plate dives beneath the South American Plate along the Pacific coast. This subduction also causes the range's many volcanoes and earthquakes.

**Inca Empire, Machu Picchu, and the Sacred Valley**
The Inca Empire was centered in the Andes, with its capital at Cusco. Machu Picchu sits above the Urubamba Valley, also called the Sacred Valley of the Incas. Andean peoples organized themselves in kinship groups called ayllu, farmed on terraces, and preserved potatoes as freeze-dried chuño.

**Altiplano**
The high plateau of the central Andes, mostly in Bolivia and Peru, home to Lake Titicaca and many Aymara people. Llamas and vicuñas live there. La Paz, Bolivia's seat of government, is on its edge and is the highest capital city in the world.

**Andean condor**
A huge vulture with a white feather collar around its neck, named after the range. It is often called the largest bird of prey in the world and is a national symbol of several Andean countries.

**Andean cock-of-the-rock**
A bright orange-red bird with black wings that lives in the cloud forests of the eastern Andes. It is the national bird of Peru. The spectacled (Andean) bear and the Andean flicker, a ground-dwelling woodpecker found in places like Bolivia's Sajama National Park, also live in the range.

**Tierra del Fuego (southern end)**
The Andes run for about 7,000 km along western South America and end in the Tierra del Fuego archipelago at the continent's southern tip. This makes them the longest continental mountain range in the world.

**Christ the Redeemer of the Andes**
A statue of Christ placed in 1904 at the high pass between Mendoza, Argentina, and Chile (the Uspallata or La Cumbre Pass), south of Aconcagua. It celebrates the peaceful settlement of a border dispute between the two countries.

**Potosí silver mines**
Cerro Rico ("Rich Hill") at Potosí, in the Bolivian Andes, was the Spanish Empire's greatest source of silver in the colonial era. The Andes are still a major mining region, with mines such as Yanacocha, a huge gold mine in Peru.

**Atacama Desert rain shadow**
The Andes block moist air from the east, which helps make the Atacama Desert of northern Chile, to the west of the range, the driest non-polar desert in the world. The Atacama region also has large lithium deposits.

**Ojos del Salado**
The highest active volcano in the world, on the Chile–Argentina border. Its name means "eyes of the salty one," after the salt lagoons on its slopes.

**Puya raimondii**
The "Queen of the Andes," the largest bromeliad in the world. It grows at high altitude in Peru and Bolivia and sends up a giant flower spike once before dying. The Andean cloud forests are also home to the cinchona tree, whose bark gave the antimalarial drug quinine.
